newsitem.title: USA: Innotech Inc holders reap neat profit.
newsitem.headline: Innotech Inc holders reap neat profit.

text.p: Shareholders who held on to Innotech Inc shares, despite a year of flat-lining, reaped a handsome 37.5 percent profit after Johnson & Johnson offered to buyout the maker of systems that can customize prescription lenses for eyeglass retailers.
Innotech went public at $10 a share in March last year. Since then, the stock has dipped slightly and risen, but remained generally close to its IPO price -- until today.
J&J, which already owned five percent of Innotech, agreed to buyout Innotech for a $13.75 a share, sending the stock soaring over 50 percent, or 4-41/64 to 13-33/64.
Profitability concerns may have hampered the stock, Wall Street analysts said, although the company was expected to get out of the red in the fourth quarter of this year.

"Management was quite frustrated. They had made all their benchmarks as far as meeting the amount of equipment, new units...and some neat innovations in eyecare," said Lehman Brothers analyst Jeffrey Kessler. "It's too bad investors didn't see what Johnson & Johnson could."
Innotech's systems are designed to allow retail optometrists to cast complex lenses of different materials in their offices more quickly and more cheaply than relying on a lens laboratory.

"Johnson & Johnson should be very successful with this. They could make this into a $100 million plus business...It's service intensive and they can quickly set up a new distribution channel," said Hambrecht & Quist analyst Robert Faulkner. One investor that stands to make quite a bundle from tendering shares is Chase Manhattan Corp, which owned just over 20 percent of Innotech as of June 1996.
